newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian army, Khmer Rouge to hold merger talks.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian army, Khmer Rouge to hold merger talks.

text.p: Generals from Cambodia's royal armed forces and dissident Khmer Rouge commanders will meet on Tuesday to discuss formally merging their two forces, Cambodian co-Premier Hun Sen said on Monday.

"Tomorrow there will be a big meeting in order to merge the government troops and the Khmer Rouge separatists," he said, without giving any more details such as the venue and the identities of those taking part.
The two sides have forged a ceasefire and the dissidents recognise the authority of the government and its struggle against the hardline Khmer Rouge.

Co-Defence Minister Tea Banh told Reuters the meeting would be held in the northwest stronghold of Pailin, close to the border with Thailand, and said the government side would be led by armed forces chief of staff General Ke Kim Yan.

Analysts said the committee would include the general's two most senior deputies, Nhek Bun Chhay and Pol Saroeun, while senior guerrilla commanders Sok Peap and Ei Chien would represent dissident Khmer Rouge leader Ieng Sary, who was given a royal pardon on Saturday.

Ieng Sary was foreign minister during Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot's 1975-79 "killing fields" regime when more than one million people died. He was sentenced to death in absentia for his role in the genocide.

Sok Peap and Ei Chien, commanders respectively of guerrilla divisions in the northwest bases of Phnom Malai and Pailin, broke from forces loyal to Pol Pot in early August and professed loyalty to Ieng Sary.
Hun Sen, speaking at the royal school of administration, also said more than two-thirds of the country's MPs had so far signed a motion approving King Norodom Sihanouk's amnesty for Ieng Sary.
Several MPs in the 120-member house said on Monday they were surprised not to have been asked for their support before the two premiers met the king on Saturday to sign the document.
Sihanouk had originally said he would only consider an amnesty for Ieng Sary on receiving written requests from the government and a two-thirds majority of assembly members.
Ieng Sary said on September 9 the government must clarify his legal status for peace talks to advance.
Hun Sen said on Saturday that the two-thirds support had been garnered, but while some MPs said they had signed an amnesty motion, others said they had yet to do so.
Ahmad Yahya, an MP of the royalist FUNCINPEC party, said he had been asked to sign the motion and added, "I support the amnesty, but I feel uncomfortable at the way they handled it."
He and other MPs said the constitution allowed for the assembly to be bypassed but if problems arose with Ieng Sary, the responsibility would be with the government and the king.
The Khmer Rouge signed a United Nations brokered peace pact in 1991 but later reneged on the acccord and have been fighting the coalition that emerged from general elections in 1993.
